preamble: Lowering and unrounding of the first element of [ui]/[ʊɪ]. In Early Modern English, the late Middle English diphthong /ʊɪ/ of boil, join, point and poison merged with /əɪ/~/aɪ/, the Great Vowel Shift reflex of Middle English /iː/, so that join rhymed with line. Standard English later restored /ɔɪ/ from spelling and regional variants, but merged forms survived in dialect speech, such as jine for join and Yola bile 'to boil'.

examples.note: Shown by rhymes such as 'join–line' in Pope and 'Mind–join'd' in Congreve; jine survives as a pronunciation spelling.
Described as a vulgar pronunciation in Ireland.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (n.d.). Line–loin merger (citing Barber, C. (1997). Early Modern English, pp. 108–116). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line%E2%80%93loin_merger
